title: Client pacing vs server burst: trace decomposition and microbench notes
content:
Goal:
Decompose end-to-end tail-latency spikes into client pacing vs server-burst behaviors and quantify the overhead contribution from TLS/TCP coalescing + intermediary proxies for streaming RPCs (HTTP/gRPC).

Background/context:
We keep seeing sporadic ~40-200ms tail spikes on small incremental-streamed responses (short generations where the server emits 1-4 chunks). Customer payloads often use HTTP chunked streaming and gRPC-server-stream with small chunk sizes (~256-1024 bytes). The hypothesis is that a non-trivial portion of observed tail is not model compute but network interactions: client TCP/TLS flush timing, proxy buffering thresholds, and server-side write batching.

High-level questions:
- How much of observed 99th/99.9th latency for short-stream requests is attributable to network/staging (client, proxy, TLS coalescing) vs server-side scheduling and KV cache warmup?
- Are HTTP chunking and gRPC streaming different in their sensitivity to client pacing?
- Does TLS record sizing and Nagle/Delayed ACK interactions amplify latency variance?
- Can we recommend mitigation knobs (client flush hints, proxy low-latency mode, server-side explicit flush after first chunk)?

Experiment design (trace decomposition):
- Workloads: synthetic single-turn prompts that produce 1, 2, or 4 incremental tokens/chunks. Small and consistent model runtime (quantized 2-bit) to minimize server compute variance.
- Clients: 3 client implementations: (A) naive Python requests-based streaming with immediate flush, (B) golang-grpc default stream client, (C) custom client that batches writes at 5ms and 20ms to emulate delayed client pacing.
- Transport: tests over direct path (no proxy), edge-proxy, and a chain with one intermediate L7 proxy + CDN-like buffering (simulate buffering thresholds).
- TLS: run with TLS enabled and disabled to observe record coalescing effects. Also toggle TCP_NODELAY, and server-side write coalesce window (0ms, 5ms, 20ms).
- Instrumentation: full packet capture (tcpdump) on client, proxy, and server; application traces with per-chunk timestamps (client-send, proxy-ingress, server-send, proxy-egress, client-recv). Collect kernel-level timestamps where possible and the TLS record boundaries from pcap.
- Metrics: per-request latency breakdown (time to first byte, inter-chunk gaps, time to final byte), distribution (p50/p90/p99/p99.9), jitter/variance, correlation between TLS record boundaries and application-observed gaps.

Quick notes on methodology pitfalls:
- Kernel timestamp resolution and asynchronous write coalescing can create ambiguity; we used SO_TIMESTAMPING on Linux where available and validated against pcap wallclock.
- Synthetic clients must mimic real-world flush patterns; we recorded production client traces to seed the pacing parameters.
- Proxy behavior is highly configuration dependent; we tested default buffering and low-latency mode where proxy flushes after small write counts.

Results summary (high level):
- Direct path (no proxy): client pacing dominates for small-chunk workloads. When client deliberately batch-delays at 20ms, median total latency increased by ~18ms and p99 by ~45ms vs immediate flush client. TCP_NODELAY avoided a ~6ms floor in a subset of cases.
- TLS on vs off: TLS introduced an extra quantized step in inter-chunk gaps correlated with TLS record coalescing. Measured additional variance up to 12ms on p99 for very small writes (~200-400B) when TLS records were coalesced into larger segments.
- Proxy chain: single L7 proxy in default config added an effective buffering delay distribution with a long tail — p99 delta of +30ms vs direct for 1-2 chunk cases. Enabling proxy low-latency mode reduced that to +6ms but increased CPU utilization by ~22%.
- HTTP chunked vs gRPC: observed behavior depended more on client write patterns than protocol semantics. gRPC (HTTP/2) multiplexing tends to coalesce more aggressively within a connection; when client flushes promptly, gRPC had marginally lower p50 but similar p99 to HTTP.
- Server-side coalesce: server write coalesce windows (emulated) when non-zero reduced CPU syscalls but shifted latency mass to the right — small coalesce (<=5ms) was an effective tradeoff; >=20ms produced unacceptable tail for interactive workloads.

Representative trace decomposition (one 2-chunk sample):
- Client app invoked write(chunk1) at t=0. Client kernel enqueues, flushes to socket at t=0.8ms.
- TLS handshake state: session resumed, no handshake. TLS record containing chunk1 left client host at t=1.5ms.
- Proxy ingress pcap shows arrival t=4.6ms; proxy buffered until threshold and flushed at t=14.2ms (default config). Proxy egress arrives at server t=18.9ms.
- Server app read -> compute (model produce chunk1) complete at t=40.5ms; server write(chunk2) leaves server kernel at t=41.2ms.
- Proxy back-path adds another 12ms buffering for chunk2 in default mode; client receives final byte at t=66.7ms.
- Application-observed gaps: first chunk latency = 40.5ms (dominated by compute), inter-chunk gap = 26.2ms (dominated by proxy buffering).

Key takeaways and actionable recommendations:
1) Client-side flushing is critical for short incremental streams. SDKs should expose a "flush immediacy" option and document default behavior per language binding. For latency-sensitive streams, default to immediate flush and TCP_NODELAY when supported.
2) Proxies must offer an explicit low-latency mode; default buffering thresholds target throughput but can hurt interactive tail. We should add a recommended config profile for our edge proxy for streaming endpoints.
3) TLS record coalescing causes quantized delays especially for very small writes. Options: (a) adjust record size thresholds in TLS stack (where possible), (b) bundle small protocol-level control frames with payload, (c) tune client-side write timing.
4) Server coalescing: small (<=5ms) server-side coalesce reduces syscall overhead without large latency penalty; expose this as a tunable with recommended defaults.
5) Docs/SDKs: ship guidelines and small code samples showing how to set flush behavior in Python/gRPC/Go. Provide a snippet that toggles TCP_NODELAY and explictly flushes after chunk writes.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How representative is our synthetic model of customers using streaming for hallucination mitigation vs full generation? Need to replay longer traces from three enterprise customers.
- Investigate kernel-level write batching heuristics and the interaction with user-space event loops (Node.js libuv, Python asyncio).
- Explore an automated probe that runs at customer edge to profile proxy configs and recommend low-latency profile when streaming is detected.

Immediate next steps:
- PR #1189 contains the test harness and pcap collection scripts — run against two more real customer traces (owner: Jing).
- Draft an internal "Streaming Latency Checklist" for Solutions Eng and customers with recommended proxy and client settings (owner: Liam).
- Prototype a proxy low-latency config toggle and measure CPU/cost impact at 10k RPS (owner: Ravi).

Appendix (notes & raw observations):
- In many traces we saw a ~8-12ms quantization step that lined up with TLS record sizing; this suggests the TLS stack coalesces user writes into records to amortize crypto costs.
- Delayed ACK interactions: in a few cross-datacenter cases a delayed ACK from client caused the server to wait for the ACK before sending the next chunk, producing a ~40ms spike. TCP_NODELAY alone did not fix this; combination of smaller writes and explicit flushes plus socket options mitigated it.
- Empirical rule of thumb from these experiments: for 1-4 chunk interactive streams, aim to keep: (client flush latency + proxy buffering) < 10ms to avoid dominating model compute (assuming model compute ~20-50ms).

Notes to self / rough TODOs (scratch):
- Re-run same matrix for HTTP/3 (quic) — early hypothesis: QUIC coalescing different behavior, might reduce some of the TLS-record quantization.
- Collect Node.js client patterns from customer SDK usage logs.
- Add a small diagram mapping where to instrument (client kernel, proxy ingress/egress, server kernel) and share in next eng sync.

If you want to reproduce locally: see linked PR for harness; recommended minimal run: 10k short-stream requests with 90/10 1-chunk/2-chunk mix, TLS on/off, proxy in default/low-latency. Save pcaps and use `trace-slice` tool (in repo) to extract per-request TLS record boundaries.

End of notes.
